hops.afterHeading: Holding the rise back, and letting it go
hops.title: A cancer drug that stops healthy cells from dividing, on purpose
hops.text: Chemotherapy is hardest on dividing cells, including the busy blood-forming cells in bone marrow. Trilaciclib protects them by stopping them from dividing, briefly. This short-acting CDK4/6 inhibitor was approved in the United States in 2021 to protect blood-cell production in adults getting certain chemotherapy for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. Given just before treatment, it holds cycling stem and progenitor cells, which still have working Rb, in G1, where they are less vulnerable. Small cell lung cancers almost always lack working Rb. With no Rb brake for the drug to hold, such tumor cells kept cycling in lab tests, and the drug did not shield them from cisplatin or etoposide.

sources.citation: Dhillon S, Trilaciclib: First Approval, Drugs 81(7):867-874, 2021

Bisi JE, Sorrentino JA, Roberts PJ, Tavares FX, Strum JC, Preclinical characterization of G1T28: a novel CDK4/6 inhibitor for reduction of chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression, Molecular Cancer Therapeutics 15(5):783-793, 2016
Keogh A, Finn S, Radonic T, Emerging biomarkers and the changing landscape of small cell lung cancer, Cancers 14(15):3772, 2022

hops.afterHeading: The fall: destruction makes it one way
hops.title: The yew tree drug that holds microtubules together
hops.text: In 1962, on the last day of a collecting trip, botanist Arthur Barclay took samples from a single Pacific yew. In a government screen of 115,000 plant extracts, its bark extract killed cells. Chemists Monroe Wall and Mansukh Wani purified the compound and named it taxol. The spindle poison colchicine blocks microtubule assembly. In 1979 Susan Horwitz's lab found that in a test tube taxol does the opposite: microtubules assemble and resist falling apart, even in the cold. At the concentrations common in lab cultures, a few kinetochores stay unattached, so the checkpoint keeps the APC/C from tagging securin and cyclin B, and cells stall in mitosis.

sources.citation: Weaver BA, How Taxol/paclitaxel kills cancer cells, Molecular Biology of the Cell 25(18):2677-2681, 2014
Schiff PB, Fant J, Horwitz SB, Promotion of microtubule assembly in vitro by taxol, Nature 277(5698):665-667, 1979

image.caption: Pacific yew bark yielded taxol, which stabilizes microtubules and can hold cells in mitosis.

hops.title: Is your whole body really replaced every seven years?
hops.text: You may have heard that every cell in your body is replaced every seven years. Cold War bomb tests showed otherwise. Above-ground nuclear tests sent carbon-14 in the atmosphere soaring, and after 1963 it fell steadily. Cells build carbon into DNA when they copy their genomes, so the carbon-14 in DNA pooled from a group of cells shows roughly when that DNA was made, a bit like an EdU pulse given to the whole planet. Neurons in the occipital cortex turned out to be as old as the person. Heart muscle cells do renew, but slowly: fewer than half are replaced in a lifetime.

sources.citation: Spalding KL, Bhardwaj RD, Buchholz BA, Druid H, Frisén J, Retrospective birth dating of cells in humans, Cell 122(1):133-143, 2005
Bergmann O, Bhardwaj RD, Bernard S, et al., Evidence for cardiomyocyte renewal in humans, Science 324(5923):98-102, 2009

image.caption: Bomb-test carbon-14 showed occipital neurons are as old as you, while heart muscle cells renew slowly.
